    77→    # If the column has info defined, we copy it and adjust any indices
    78→    # to point to the copied column.  By guarding with the if statement,
    79→    # we avoid side effects (of creating the default info instance).
    80→    if 'info' in col.__dict__:
    81→        newcol.info = col.info
    82→        if copy_indices and col.info.indices:
    83→            newcol.info.indices = deepcopy(col.info.indices)

    85→                index.replace_col(col, newcol)

   117→def _expand_string_array_for_values(arr, values):
   118→    """
   119→    For string-dtype return a version of ``arr`` that is wide enough for ``values``.
   120→    If ``arr`` is not string-dtype or does not need expansion then return ``arr``.
   121→
   122→    Parameters
   123→    ----------
   124→    arr : np.ndarray
   125→        Input array
   126→    values : scalar or array-like
   127→        Values for width comparison for string arrays
   128→
   129→    Returns
   130→    -------
   131→    arr_expanded : np.ndarray
   132→
   133→    """
   134→    if arr.dtype.kind in ('U', 'S') and values is not np.ma.masked:
   135→        # Find the length of the longest string in the new values.
   136→        values_str_len = np.char.str_len(values).max()
   137→
   138→        # Determine character repeat count of arr.dtype.  Returns a positive
   139→        # int or None (something like 'U0' is not possible in numpy).  If new values
   140→        # are longer than current then make a new (wider) version of arr.
   141→        arr_str_len = dtype_bytes_or_chars(arr.dtype)
   142→        if arr_str_len and values_str_len > arr_str_len:
   143→            arr_dtype = arr.dtype.byteorder + arr.dtype.kind + str(values_str_len)
   144→            arr = arr.astype(arr_dtype)
   145→
   146→    return arr

   149→def _convert_sequence_data_to_array(data, dtype=None):
   150→    """Convert N-d sequence-like data to ndarray or MaskedArray.
   151→
   152→    This is the core function for converting Python lists or list of lists to a
   153→    numpy array. This handles embedded np.ma.masked constants in ``data`` along
   154→    with the special case of an homogeneous list of MaskedArray elements.
   155→
   156→    Considerations:
   157→
   158→    - np.ma.array is about 50 times slower than np.array for list input. This
   159→      function avoids using np.ma.array on list input.
   160→    - np.array emits a UserWarning for embedded np.ma.masked, but only for int
   161→      or float inputs. For those it converts to np.nan and forces float dtype.
   162→      For other types np.array is inconsistent, for instance converting
   163→      np.ma.masked to "0.0" for str types.
   164→    - Searching in pure Python for np.ma.masked in ``data`` is comparable in
   165→      speed to calling ``np.array(data)``.
   166→    - This function may end up making two additional copies of input ``data``.
   167→
   168→    Parameters
   169→    ----------
   170→    data : N-d sequence
   171→        Input data, typically list or list of lists
   172→    dtype : None or dtype-like
   173→        Output datatype (None lets np.array choose)
   174→
   175→    Returns
   176→    -------
   177→    np_data : np.ndarray or np.ma.MaskedArray
   178→
   179→    """
   180→    np_ma_masked = np.ma.masked  # Avoid repeated lookups of this object
   181→
   182→    # Special case of an homogeneous list of MaskedArray elements (see #8977).
   183→    # np.ma.masked is an instance of MaskedArray, so exclude those values.
   184→    if (hasattr(data, '__len__')
   185→        and len(data) > 0
   186→        and all(isinstance(val, np.ma.MaskedArray)
   187→                and val is not np_ma_masked for val in data)):
   188→        np_data = np.ma.array(data, dtype=dtype)
   189→        return np_data
   190→
   191→    # First convert data to a plain ndarray. If there are instances of np.ma.masked
   192→    # in the data this will issue a warning for int and float.
   193→    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as warns:
   194→        # Ensure this warning from numpy is always enabled and that it is not
   195→        # converted to an error (which can happen during pytest).
   196→        warnings.filterwarnings('always', category=UserWarning,
   197→                                message='.*converting a masked element.*')
   198→        # FutureWarning in numpy 1.21. See https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/11291
   199→        # and https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/18425.
   200→        warnings.filterwarnings('always', category=FutureWarning,
   201→                                message='.*Promotion of numbers and bools to strings.*')
   202→        try:
   203→            np_data = np.array(data, dtype=dtype)
   204→        except np.ma.MaskError:
   205→            # Catches case of dtype=int with masked values, instead let it
   206→            # convert to float
   207→            np_data = np.array(data)
   208→        except Exception:
   209→            # Conversion failed for some reason, e.g. [2, 1*u.m] gives TypeError in Quantity.
   210→            # First try to interpret the data as Quantity. If that still fails then fall
   211→            # through to object
   212→            try:
   213→                np_data = Quantity(data, dtype)
   214→            except Exception:
   215→                dtype = object
   216→                np_data = np.array(data, dtype=dtype)
   217→
   218→    if np_data.ndim == 0 or (np_data.ndim > 0 and len(np_data) == 0):
   219→        # Implies input was a scalar or an empty list (e.g. initializing an
   220→        # empty table with pre-declared names and dtypes but no data).  Here we
   221→        # need to fall through to initializing with the original data=[].
   222→        return data
   223→
   224→    # If there were no warnings and the data are int or float, then we are done.
   225→    # Other dtypes like string or complex can have masked values and the
   226→    # np.array() conversion gives the wrong answer (e.g. converting np.ma.masked
   227→    # to the string "0.0").
   228→    if len(warns) == 0 and np_data.dtype.kind in ('i', 'f'):
   229→        return np_data
   230→
   231→    # Now we need to determine if there is an np.ma.masked anywhere in input data.
   232→
   233→    # Make a statement like below to look for np.ma.masked in a nested sequence.
   234→    # Because np.array(data) succeeded we know that `data` has a regular N-d
   235→    # structure. Find ma_masked:
   236→    #   any(any(any(d2 is ma_masked for d2 in d1) for d1 in d0) for d0 in data)
   237→    # Using this eval avoids creating a copy of `data` in the more-usual case of
   238→    # no masked elements.
   239→    any_statement = 'd0 is ma_masked'
   240→    for ii in reversed(range(np_data.ndim)):
   241→        if ii == 0:
   242→            any_statement = f'any({any_statement} for d0 in data)'
   243→        elif ii == np_data.ndim - 1:
   244→            any_statement = f'any(d{ii} is ma_masked for d{ii} in d{ii-1})'
   245→        else:
   246→            any_statement = f'any({any_statement} for d{ii} in d{ii-1})'
   247→    context = {'ma_masked': np.ma.masked, 'data': data}
   248→    has_masked = eval(any_statement, context)
   249→
   250→    # If there are any masks then explicitly change each one to a fill value and
   251→    # set a mask boolean array. If not has_masked then we're done.
   252→    if has_masked:
   253→        mask = np.zeros(np_data.shape, dtype=bool)
   254→        data_filled = np.array(data, dtype=object)
   255→
   256→        # Make type-appropriate fill value based on initial conversion.
   257→        if np_data.dtype.kind == 'U':
   258→            fill = ''
   259→        elif np_data.dtype.kind == 'S':
   260→            fill = b''
   261→        else:
   262→            # Zero works for every numeric type.
   263→            fill = 0
   264→
   265→        ranges = [range(dim) for dim in np_data.shape]
   266→        for idxs in itertools.product(*ranges):
   267→            val = data_filled[idxs]
   268→            if val is np_ma_masked:
   269→                data_filled[idxs] = fill
   270→                mask[idxs] = True
   271→            elif isinstance(val, bool) and dtype is None:
   272→                # If we see a bool and dtype not specified then assume bool for
   273→                # the entire array. Not perfect but in most practical cases OK.
   274→                # Unfortunately numpy types [False, 0] as int, not bool (and
   275→                # [False, np.ma.masked] => array([0.0, np.nan])).
   276→                dtype = bool
   277→
   278→        # If no dtype is provided then need to convert back to list so np.array
   279→        # does type autodetection.
   280→        if dtype is None:
   281→            data_filled = data_filled.tolist()
   282→
   283→        # Use np.array first to convert `data` to ndarray (fast) and then make
   284→        # masked array from an ndarray with mask (fast) instead of from `data`.
   285→        np_data = np.ma.array(np.array(data_filled, dtype=dtype), mask=mask)
   286→
   287→    return np_data

   290→def _make_compare(oper):
   291→    """
   292→    Make Column comparison methods which encode the ``other`` object to utf-8
   293→    in the case of a bytestring dtype for Py3+.
   294→
   295→    Parameters
   296→    ----------
   297→    oper : str
   298→        Operator name
   299→    """
   300→    def _compare(self, other):
   301→        op = oper  # copy enclosed ref to allow swap below
   302→
   303→        # If other is a Quantity, we should let it do the work, since
   304→        # it can deal with our possible unit (which, for MaskedColumn,
   305→        # would get dropped below, as '.data' is accessed in super()).
   306→        if isinstance(other, Quantity):
   307→            return NotImplemented
   308→
   309→        # If we are unicode and other is a column with bytes, defer to it for
   310→        # doing the unicode sandwich.  This avoids problems like those
   311→        # discussed in #6838 and #6899.
   312→        if (self.dtype.kind == 'U'
   313→                and isinstance(other, Column) and other.dtype.kind == 'S'):
   314→            return NotImplemented
   315→
   316→        # If we are bytes, encode other as needed.
   317→        if self.dtype.char == 'S':
   318→            other = self._encode_str(other)
   319→
   320→        # Now just let the regular ndarray.__eq__, etc., take over.
   321→        result = getattr(super(Column, self), op)(other)
   322→        # But we should not return Column instances for this case.
   323→        return result.data if isinstance(result, Column) else result
   324→
   325→    return _compare

   328→class ColumnInfo(BaseColumnInfo):
   329→    """
   330→    Container for meta information like name, description, format.
   331→
   332→    This is required when the object is used as a mixin column within a table,
   333→    but can be used as a general way to store meta information.
   334→    """
   335→    attr_names = BaseColumnInfo.attr_names | {'groups'}
   336→    _attrs_no_copy = BaseColumnInfo._attrs_no_copy | {'groups'}
   337→    attrs_from_parent = attr_names
   338→    _supports_indexing = True
   339→    # For structured columns, data is used to store a dict of columns.
   340→    # Store entries in that dict as name.key instead of name.data.key.
   341→    _represent_as_dict_primary_data = 'data'
   342→
   343→    def _represent_as_dict(self):
   344→        result = super()._represent_as_dict()
   345→        names = self._parent.dtype.names
   346→        # For a regular column, we are done, but for a structured
   347→        # column, we use a SerializedColumns to store the pieces.
   348→        if names is None:
   349→            return result
   350→
   351→        from .serialize import SerializedColumn
   352→
   353→        data = SerializedColumn()
   354→        # If this column has a StructuredUnit, we split it and store
   355→        # it on the corresponding part. Otherwise, we just store it
   356→        # as an attribute below.  All other attributes we remove from
   357→        # the parts, so that we do not store them multiple times.
   358→        # (Note that attributes are not linked to the parent, so it
   359→        # is safe to reset them.)
   360→        # TODO: deal with (some of) this in Column.__getitem__?
   361→        # Alternatively: should we store info on the first part?
   362→        # TODO: special-case format somehow? Can we have good formats
   363→        # for structured columns?
   364→        unit = self.unit
   365→        if isinstance(unit, StructuredUnit) and len(unit) == len(names):
   366→            units = unit.values()
   367→            unit = None  # No need to store as an attribute as well.
   368→        else:
   369→            units = [None] * len(names)
   370→        for name, part_unit in zip(names, units):
   371→            part = self._parent[name]
   372→            part.unit = part_unit
   373→            part.description = None
   374→            part.meta = {}
   375→            part.format = None
   376→            data[name] = part
   377→
   378→        # Create the attributes required to reconstruct the column.
   379→        result['data'] = data
   380→        # Store the shape if needed. Just like scalar data, a structured data
   381→        # column (e.g. with dtype `f8,i8`) can be multidimensional within each
   382→        # row and have a shape, and that needs to be distinguished from the
   383→        # case that each entry in the structure has the same shape (e.g.,
   384→        # distinguist a column with dtype='f8,i8' and 2 elements per row from
   385→        # one with dtype '2f8,2i8' and just one element per row).
   386→        if shape := self._parent.shape[1:]:
   387→            result['shape'] = list(shape)
   388→        # Also store the standard info attributes since these are
   389→        # stored on the parent and can thus just be passed on as
   390→        # arguments.  TODO: factor out with essentially the same
   391→        # code in serialize._represent_mixin_as_column.
   392→        if unit is not None and unit != '':
   393→            result['unit'] = unit
   394→        if self.format is not None:
   395→            result['format'] = self.format
   396→        if self.description is not None:
   397→            result['description'] = self.description
   398→        if self.meta:
   399→            result['meta'] = self.meta
   400→
   401→        return result

   403→    def _construct_from_dict(self, map):
   404→        if not isinstance(map.get('data'), dict):
   405→            return super()._construct_from_dict(map)
   406→
   407→        # Reconstruct a structured Column, by first making an empty column
   408→        # and then filling it with the structured data.
   409→        data = map.pop('data')
   410→        shape = tuple(map.pop('shape', ()))
   411→        # There are three elements in the shape of `part`:
   412→        # (table length, shape of structured column, shape of part like '3f8')
   413→        # The column `shape` only includes the second, so by adding one to its
   414→        # length to include the table length, we pick off a possible last bit.
   415→        dtype = np.dtype([(name, part.dtype, part.shape[len(shape)+1:])
   416→                          for name, part in data.items()])
   417→        units = tuple(col.info.unit for col in data.values())
   418→        if all(unit is not None for unit in units):
   419→            map['unit'] = StructuredUnit(units, dtype)
   420→        map.update(dtype=dtype, shape=shape, length=len(data[dtype.names[0]]))
   421→        # Construct the empty column from `map` (note: 'data' removed above).
   422→        result = super()._construct_from_dict(map)
   423→        # Fill it with the structured data.
   424→        for name in dtype.names:
   425→            result[name] = data[name]
   426→        return result

   561→    def copy(self, order='C', data=None, copy_data=True):
   562→        """
   563→        Return a copy of the current instance.
   564→
   565→        If ``data`` is supplied then a view (reference) of ``data`` is used,
   566→        and ``copy_data`` is ignored.
   567→
   568→        Parameters
   569→        ----------
   570→        order : {'C', 'F', 'A', 'K'}, optional
   571→            Controls the memory layout of the copy. 'C' means C-order,
   572→            'F' means F-order, 'A' means 'F' if ``a`` is Fortran contiguous,
   573→            'C' otherwise. 'K' means match the layout of ``a`` as closely
   574→            as possible. (Note that this function and :func:numpy.copy are very
   575→            similar, but have different default values for their order=
   576→            arguments.)  Default is 'C'.
   577→        data : array, optional
   578→            If supplied then use a view of ``data`` instead of the instance
   579→            data.  This allows copying the instance attributes and meta.
   580→        copy_data : bool, optional
   581→            Make a copy of the internal numpy array instead of using a
   582→            reference.  Default is True.
   583→

   585→        -------
   586→        col : Column or MaskedColumn
   587→            Copy of the current column (same type as original)

   590→            data = self.data
   591→            if copy_data:
   592→                data = data.copy(order)
   593→
   594→        out = data.view(self.__class__)
   595→        out.__array_finalize__(self)
   596→
   597→        # If there is meta on the original column then deepcopy (since "copy" of column
   598→        # implies complete independence from original).  __array_finalize__ will have already
   599→        # made a light copy.  I'm not sure how to avoid that initial light copy.
   600→        if self.meta is not None:
   601→            out.meta = self.meta  # MetaData descriptor does a deepcopy here

   612→    def __setstate__(self, state):
   613→        """
   614→        Restore the internal state of the Column/MaskedColumn for pickling
   615→        purposes.  This requires that the last element of ``state`` is a
   616→        5-tuple that has Column-specific state values.
   617→        """
   618→        # Get the Column attributes
   619→        names = ('_name', '_unit', '_format', 'description', 'meta', 'indices')
   620→        attrs = {name: val for name, val in zip(names, state[-1])}
   621→
   622→        state = state[:-1]
   623→

   625→        # "TypeError 'int' object is not iterable", raised in
   626→        # astropy.table._column_mixins._ColumnGetitemShim.__setstate_cython__()
   627→        # Previously, it seems to have given an infinite recursion.
   628→        # Hence, manually call the right super class to actually set up
   629→        # the array object.
   630→        super_class = ma.MaskedArray if isinstance(self, ma.MaskedArray) else np.ndarray
   631→        super_class.__setstate__(self, state)

   638→    def __reduce__(self):

   641→        functionality but then add in a 5-tuple of Column-specific values
   642→        that get used in __setstate__.

   644→        super_class = ma.MaskedArray if isinstance(self, ma.MaskedArray) else np.ndarray
   645→        reconstruct_func, reconstruct_func_args, state = super_class.__reduce__(self)
   646→
   647→        # Define Column-specific attrs and meta that gets added to state.
   648→        column_state = (self.name, self.unit, self.format, self.description,
   649→                        self.meta, self.indices)
   650→        state = state + (column_state,)

   652→        return reconstruct_func, reconstruct_func_args, state

   654→    def __array_finalize__(self, obj):

   672→    def __array_wrap__(self, out_arr, context=None):
   673→        """
   674→        __array_wrap__ is called at the end of every ufunc.
   675→
   676→        Normally, we want a Column object back and do not have to do anything
   677→        special. But there are two exceptions:
   678→

   680→           like sum() or mean()), a Column still linking to a parent_table
   681→           makes little sense, so we return the output viewed as the
   682→           column content (ndarray or MaskedArray).

   685→           returns a zero rank scalar array while np.mean() returns a scalar;

   689→           we also want to consistently return an array rather than a column

   692→        out_arr = super().__array_wrap__(out_arr, context)
   693→        if (self.shape != out_arr.shape
   694→            or (isinstance(out_arr, BaseColumn)
   695→                and (context is not None
   696→                     and context[0] in _comparison_functions))):
   697→            return out_arr.data[()]
   698→        else:
   699→            return out_arr

  1060→    @staticmethod

  1064→        called for Py3+.

  1069→            pass

  1087→class Column(BaseColumn):

  1102→    description : str or None

  1104→    unit : str or None

  1106→    format : str, None, or callable

  1108→        "old-style" (``format % value``) or "new-style" (`str.format`)
  1109→        format specification string or a function or any callable object that
  1110→        accepts a single value and returns a string.

  1115→    --------
  1116→    A Column can be created in two different ways:
  1117→
  1118→    - Provide a ``data`` value but not ``shape`` or ``length`` (which are
  1119→      inferred from the data).
  1120→
  1121→      Examples::
  1122→
  1123→        col = Column(data=[1, 2], name='name')  # shape=(2,)
  1124→        col = Column(data=[[1, 2], [3, 4]], name='name')  # shape=(2, 2)
  1125→        col = Column(data=[1, 2], name='name', dtype=float)
  1126→        col = Column(data=np.array([1, 2]), name='name')
  1127→        col = Column(data=['hello', 'world'], name='name')

  1130→      fixed-size data-type initializer for the numpy.dtype() method.  See
  1131→      `<https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/arrays.dtypes.html>`_.
  1132→      Examples include:
  1133→
  1134→      - Python non-string type (float, int, bool)
  1135→      - Numpy non-string type (e.g. np.float32, np.int64, np.bool\\_)

  1139→      ``np.array(data)``.

  1142→

  1144→

  1149→      array shape of a single cell in the column.

  1152→    one of the ``data`` or ``value`` attributes (which are equivalent)::
  1153→

4. User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
5. After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as todos
6. When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work. Ideally you should only have one todo as in_progress at a time
7. After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

1. There is only a single, straightforward task
2. The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit

attributes.llm.request.functions.12.name: EnterPlanMode
attributes.llm.request.functions.12.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Task tool with explore agent instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using Glob, Grep, and Read tools
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

    61→class CsvWriter:

   295→class BaseInputter:
   296→    """

   302→    """Encoding used to read the file"""

   304→    def get_lines(self, table, newline=None):
   305→        """
   306→        Get the lines from the ``table`` input. The input table can be one of:
   307→
   308→        * File name
   309→        * String (newline separated) with all header and data lines (must have at least 2 lines)
   310→        * File-like object with read() method
   311→        * List of strings
   312→

   314→        ----------
   315→        table : str, file-like, list
   316→            Can be either a file name, string (newline separated) with all header and data
   317→            lines (must have at least 2 lines), a file-like object with a
   318→            ``read()`` method, or a list of strings.
   319→        newline :
   320→            Line separator. If `None` use OS default from ``splitlines()``.
   321→
   322→        Returns
   323→        -------
   324→        lines : list
   325→            List of lines
   326→        """
   327→        try:
   328→            if (hasattr(table, 'read')
   329→                    or ('\n' not in table + '' and '\r' not in table + '')):
   330→                with get_readable_fileobj(table,
   331→                                          encoding=self.encoding) as fileobj:
   332→                    table = fileobj.read()

   334→                lines = table.splitlines()
   335→            else:
   336→                lines = table.split(newline)
   337→        except TypeError:
   338→            try:
   339→                # See if table supports indexing, slicing, and iteration
   340→                table[0]
   341→                table[0:1]
   342→                iter(table)
   343→                if len(table) > 1:
   344→                    lines = table
   345→                else:
   346→                    # treat single entry as if string had been passed directly
   347→                    if newline is None:
   348→                        lines = table[0].splitlines()
   349→                    else:
   350→                        lines = table[0].split(newline)
   351→
   352→            except TypeError:
   353→                raise TypeError(
   354→                    'Input "table" must be a string (filename or data) or an iterable')
   355→
   356→        return self.process_lines(lines)

   365→        input lines to the table rows.  For example the

   371→class BaseSplitter:
   372→    """
   373→    Base splitter that uses python's split method to do the work.
   374→
   375→    This does not handle quoted values.  A key feature is the formulation of
   376→    __call__ as a generator that returns a list of the split line values at
   377→    each iteration.
   378→
   379→    There are two methods that are intended to be overridden, first
   380→    ``process_line()`` to do pre-processing on each input line before splitting
   381→    and ``process_val()`` to do post-processing on each split string value.  By
   382→    default these apply the string ``strip()`` function.  These can be set to
   383→    another function via the instance attribute or be disabled entirely, for
   384→    example::
   385→
   386→      reader.header.splitter.process_val = lambda x: x.lstrip()
   387→      reader.data.splitter.process_val = None
   388→
   389→    """
   390→
   391→    delimiter = None
   392→    """ one-character string used to separate fields """
   393→
   394→    def process_line(self, line):
   395→        """Remove whitespace at the beginning or end of line.  This is especially useful for
   396→        whitespace-delimited files to prevent spurious columns at the beginning or end."""
   397→        return line.strip()
   398→
   399→    def process_val(self, val):
   400→        """Remove whitespace at the beginning or end of value."""
   401→        return val.strip()
   402→
   403→    def __call__(self, lines):
   404→        if self.process_line:
   405→            lines = (self.process_line(x) for x in lines)
   406→        for line in lines:
   407→            vals = line.split(self.delimiter)
   408→            if self.process_val:
   409→                yield [self.process_val(x) for x in vals]
   410→            else:
   411→                yield vals
   412→
   413→    def join(self, vals):
   414→        if self.delimiter is None:
   415→            delimiter = ' '
   416→        else:
   417→            delimiter = self.delimiter
   418→        return delimiter.join(str(x) for x in vals)
   419→

   421→class DefaultSplitter(BaseSplitter):
   422→    """Default class to split strings into columns using python csv.  The class
   423→    attributes are taken from the csv Dialect class.
   424→
   425→    Typical usage::
   426→
   427→      # lines = ..
   428→      splitter = ascii.DefaultSplitter()
   429→      for col_vals in splitter(lines):
   430→          for col_val in col_vals:
   431→               ...
   432→
   433→    """
   434→    delimiter = ' '
   435→    """ one-character string used to separate fields. """
   436→    quotechar = '"'
   437→    """ control how instances of *quotechar* in a field are quoted """
   438→    doublequote = True
   439→    """ character to remove special meaning from following character """
   440→    escapechar = None
   441→    """ one-character stringto quote fields containing special characters """
   442→    quoting = csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL
   443→    """ control when quotes are recognized by the reader """
   444→    skipinitialspace = True
   445→    """ ignore whitespace immediately following the delimiter """
   446→    csv_writer = None
   447→    csv_writer_out = StringIO()
   448→
   449→    def process_line(self, line):
   450→        """Remove whitespace at the beginning or end of line.  This is especially useful for
   451→        whitespace-delimited files to prevent spurious columns at the beginning or end.
   452→        If splitting on whitespace then replace unquoted tabs with space first"""
   453→        if self.delimiter == r'\s':
   454→            line = _replace_tab_with_space(line, self.escapechar, self.quotechar)
   455→        return line.strip() + '\n'
   456→
   457→    def process_val(self, val):
   458→        """Remove whitespace at the beginning or end of value."""
   459→        return val.strip(' \t')
   460→
   461→    def __call__(self, lines):
   462→        """Return an iterator over the table ``lines``, where each iterator output
   463→        is a list of the split line values.
   464→
   465→        Parameters
   466→        ----------
   467→        lines : list
   468→            List of table lines
   469→
   470→        Yields
   471→        ------
   472→        line : list of str
   473→            Each line's split values.
   474→
   475→        """
   476→        if self.process_line:
   477→            lines = [self.process_line(x) for x in lines]
   478→
   479→        delimiter = ' ' if self.delimiter == r'\s' else self.delimiter
   480→
   481→        csv_reader = csv.reader(lines,
   482→                                delimiter=delimiter,
   483→                                doublequote=self.doublequote,
   484→                                escapechar=self.escapechar,
   485→                                quotechar=self.quotechar,
   486→                                quoting=self.quoting,
   487→                                skipinitialspace=self.skipinitialspace
   488→                                )
   489→        for vals in csv_reader:
   490→            if self.process_val:
   491→                yield [self.process_val(x) for x in vals]
   492→            else:
   493→                yield vals
   494→
   495→    def join(self, vals):
   496→
   497→        delimiter = ' ' if self.delimiter is None else str(self.delimiter)
   498→
   499→        if self.csv_writer is None:
   500→            self.csv_writer = CsvWriter(delimiter=delimiter,
   501→                                        doublequote=self.doublequote,
   502→                                        escapechar=self.escapechar,
   503→                                        quotechar=self.quotechar,
   504→                                        quoting=self.quoting)
   505→        if self.process_val:
   506→            vals = [self.process_val(x) for x in vals]
   507→        out = self.csv_writer.writerow(vals).rstrip('\r\n')
   508→
   509→        return out
   510→
   511→
   512→def _replace_tab_with_space(line, escapechar, quotechar):
   513→    """Replace tabs with spaces in given string, preserving quoted substrings
   514→
   515→    Parameters
   516→    ----------
   517→    line : str
   518→        String containing tabs to be replaced with spaces.
   519→    escapechar : str
   520→        Character in ``line`` used to escape special characters.
   521→    quotechar : str
   522→        Character in ``line`` indicating the start/end of a substring.
   523→
   524→    Returns
   525→    -------
   526→    line : str
   527→        A copy of ``line`` with tabs replaced by spaces, preserving quoted substrings.
   528→    """
   529→    newline = []
   530→    in_quote = False
   531→    lastchar = 'NONE'
   532→    for char in line:
   533→        if char == quotechar and lastchar != escapechar:
   534→            in_quote = not in_quote
   535→        if char == '\t' and not in_quote:
   536→            char = ' '
   537→        lastchar = char
   538→        newline.append(char)
   539→    return ''.join(newline)

   542→def _get_line_index(line_or_func, lines):
   543→    """Return the appropriate line index, depending on ``line_or_func`` which
   544→    can be either a function, a positive or negative int, or None.
   545→    """
   546→
   547→    if hasattr(line_or_func, '__call__'):
   548→        return line_or_func(lines)
   549→    elif line_or_func:
   550→        if line_or_func >= 0:
   551→            return line_or_func
   552→        else:
   553→            n_lines = sum(1 for line in lines)
   554→            return n_lines + line_or_func
   555→    else:
   556→        return line_or_func

   559→class BaseHeader:
   560→    """
   561→    Base table header reader
   562→    """
   563→    auto_format = 'col{}'
   564→    """ format string for auto-generating column names """
   565→    start_line = None
   566→    """ None, int, or a function of ``lines`` that returns None or int """
   567→    comment = None
   568→    """ regular expression for comment lines """
   569→    splitter_class = DefaultSplitter
   570→    """ Splitter class for splitting data lines into columns """
   571→    names = None
   572→    """ list of names corresponding to each data column """
   573→    write_comment = False
   574→    write_spacer_lines = ['ASCII_TABLE_WRITE_SPACER_LINE']

   576→    def __init__(self):
   577→        self.splitter = self.splitter_class()
   578→
   579→    def _set_cols_from_names(self):
   580→        self.cols = [Column(name=x) for x in self.names]

   582→    def update_meta(self, lines, meta):
   583→        """
   584→        Extract any table-level metadata, e.g. keywords, comments, column metadata, from
   585→        the table ``lines`` and update the OrderedDict ``meta`` in place.  This base
   586→        method extracts comment lines and stores them in ``meta`` for output.
   587→        """
   588→        if self.comment:
   589→            re_comment = re.compile(self.comment)
   590→            comment_lines = [x for x in lines if re_comment.match(x)]
   591→        else:
   592→            comment_lines = []
   593→        comment_lines = [re.sub('^' + self.comment, '', x).strip()
   594→                         for x in comment_lines]
   595→        if comment_lines:
   596→            meta.setdefault('table', {})['comments'] = comment_lines
   597→
   598→    def get_cols(self, lines):
   599→        """Initialize the header Column objects from the table ``lines``.
   600→
   601→        Based on the previously set Header attributes find or create the column names.
   602→        Sets ``self.cols`` with the list of Columns.
   603→
   604→        Parameters
   605→        ----------
   606→        lines : list
   607→            List of table lines
   608→
   609→        """
   610→
   611→        start_line = _get_line_index(self.start_line, self.process_lines(lines))
   612→        if start_line is None:
   613→            # No header line so auto-generate names from n_data_cols
   614→            # Get the data values from the first line of table data to determine n_data_cols
   615→            try:
   616→                first_data_vals = next(self.data.get_str_vals())
   617→            except StopIteration:
   618→                raise InconsistentTableError('No data lines found so cannot autogenerate '
   619→                                             'column names')
   620→            n_data_cols = len(first_data_vals)
   621→            self.names = [self.auto_format.format(i)
   622→                          for i in range(1, n_data_cols + 1)]
   623→
   624→        else:
   625→            for i, line in enumerate(self.process_lines(lines)):
   626→                if i == start_line:
   627→                    break
   628→            else:  # No header line matching
   629→                raise ValueError('No header line found in table')
   630→
   631→            self.names = next(self.splitter([line]))
   632→
   633→        self._set_cols_from_names()
   634→
   635→    def process_lines(self, lines):
   636→        """Generator to yield non-blank and non-comment lines"""
   637→        re_comment = re.compile(self.comment) if self.comment else None
   638→        # Yield non-comment lines
   639→        for line in lines:
   640→            if line.strip() and (not self.comment or not re_comment.match(line)):
   641→                yield line
   642→
   643→    def write_comments(self, lines, meta):
   644→        if self.write_comment not in (False, None):
   645→            for comment in meta.get('comments', []):
   646→                lines.append(self.write_comment + comment)

   648→    def write(self, lines):
   649→        if self.start_line is not None:
   650→            for i, spacer_line in zip(range(self.start_line),
   651→                                      itertools.cycle(self.write_spacer_lines)):
   652→                lines.append(spacer_line)
   653→            lines.append(self.splitter.join([x.info.name for x in self.cols]))

   655→    @property
   656→    def colnames(self):

   659→                     for col in self.cols)

   661→    def remove_columns(self, names):
   662→        """

   664→

   666→        ----------
   667→        names : list
   668→            A list containing the names of the columns to remove

   670→        colnames = self.colnames
   671→        for name in names:
   672→            if name not in colnames:

   677→    def rename_column(self, name, new_name):

   682→        ----------
   683→        name : str

   685→        new_name : str
   686→            The new name for the column
   687→        """
   688→        try:
   689→            idx = self.colnames.index(name)

   692→
   693→        col = self.cols[idx]

   703→    def get_type_map_key(self, col):

   714→    def check_column_names(self, names, strict_names, guessing):
   715→        """
   716→        Check column names.
   717→

   719→        so that guessing will fail appropriately if ``names`` is supplied.
   720→        For instance if the basic reader is given a table with no column header
   721→        row.
   722→
   723→        Parameters
   724→        ----------
   725→        names : list
   726→            User-supplied list of column names
   727→        strict_names : bool
   728→            Whether to impose extra requirements on names
   729→        guessing : bool
   730→            True if this method is being called while guessing the table format
   731→        """
   732→        if strict_names:
   733→            # Impose strict requirements on column names (normally used in guessing)
   734→            bads = [" ", ",", "|", "\t", "'", '"']
   735→            for name in self.colnames:
   736→                if (_is_number(name) or len(name) == 0
   737→                        or name[0] in bads or name[-1] in bads):
   738→                    raise InconsistentTableError(
   739→                        f'Column name {name!r} does not meet strict name requirements')
   740→        # When guessing require at least two columns, except for ECSV which can
   741→        # reliably be guessed from the header requirements.
   742→        if guessing and len(self.colnames) <= 1 and self.__class__.__name__ != 'EcsvHeader':
   743→            raise ValueError('Table format guessing requires at least two columns, got {}'
   744→                             .format(list(self.colnames)))
   745→
   746→        if names is not None and len(names) != len(self.colnames):
   747→            raise InconsistentTableError(
   748→                'Length of names argument ({}) does not match number'
   749→                ' of table columns ({})'.format(len(names), len(self.colnames)))

   752→class BaseData:

   758→    end_line = None
   759→    """ None, int, or a function of ``lines`` that returns None or int """
   760→    comment = None
   761→    """ Regular expression for comment lines """
   762→    splitter_class = DefaultSplitter
   763→    """ Splitter class for splitting data lines into columns """
   764→    write_spacer_lines = ['ASCII_TABLE_WRITE_SPACER_LINE']
   765→    fill_include_names = None
   766→    fill_exclude_names = None
   767→    fill_values = [(masked, '')]

   770→    def __init__(self):
   771→        # Need to make sure fill_values list is instance attribute, not class attribute.
   772→        # On read, this will be overwritten by the default in the ui.read (thus, in
   773→        # the current implementation there can be no different default for different
   774→        # Readers). On write, ui.py does not specify a default, so this line here matters.
   775→        self.fill_values = copy.copy(self.fill_values)
   776→        self.formats = copy.copy(self.formats)
   777→        self.splitter = self.splitter_class()

   779→    def process_lines(self, lines):
   780→        """
   781→        READ: Strip out comment lines and blank lines from list of ``lines``
   782→
   783→        Parameters
   784→        ----------
   785→        lines : list
   786→            All lines in table
   787→
   788→        Returns
   789→        -------
   790→        lines : list
   791→            List of lines
   792→
   793→        """
   794→        nonblank_lines = (x for x in lines if x.strip())
   795→        if self.comment:
   796→            re_comment = re.compile(self.comment)
   797→            return [x for x in nonblank_lines if not re_comment.match(x)]
   798→        else:
   799→            return [x for x in nonblank_lines]
   800→
   801→    def get_data_lines(self, lines):
   802→        """READ: Set ``data_lines`` attribute to lines slice comprising table data values.
   803→        """
   804→        data_lines = self.process_lines(lines)
   805→        start_line = _get_line_index(self.start_line, data_lines)
   806→        end_line = _get_line_index(self.end_line, data_lines)
   807→
   808→        if start_line is not None or end_line is not None:
   809→            self.data_lines = data_lines[slice(start_line, end_line)]
   810→        else:  # Don't copy entire data lines unless necessary
   811→            self.data_lines = data_lines
   812→
   813→    def get_str_vals(self):
   814→        """Return a generator that returns a list of column values (as strings)
   815→        for each data line."""
   816→        return self.splitter(self.data_lines)

   818→    def masks(self, cols):
   819→        """READ: Set fill value for each column and then apply that fill value
   820→
   821→        In the first step it is evaluated with value from ``fill_values`` applies to
   822→        which column using ``fill_include_names`` and ``fill_exclude_names``.
   823→        In the second step all replacements are done for the appropriate columns.
   824→        """
   825→        if self.fill_values:
   826→            self._set_fill_values(cols)
   827→            self._set_masks(cols)
   828→
   829→    def _set_fill_values(self, cols):
   830→        """READ, WRITE: Set fill values of individual cols based on fill_values of BaseData
   831→
   832→        fill values has the following form:
   833→        <fill_spec> = (<bad_value>, <fill_value>, <optional col_name>...)
   834→        fill_values = <fill_spec> or list of <fill_spec>'s
   835→
   836→        """
   837→        if self.fill_values:
   838→            # when we write tables the columns may be astropy.table.Columns
   839→            # which don't carry a fill_values by default
   840→            for col in cols:
   841→                if not hasattr(col, 'fill_values'):
   842→                    col.fill_values = {}
   843→
   844→            # if input is only one <fill_spec>, then make it a list
   845→            with suppress(TypeError):
   846→                self.fill_values[0] + ''
   847→                self.fill_values = [self.fill_values]
   848→
   849→            # Step 1: Set the default list of columns which are affected by
   850→            # fill_values
   851→            colnames = set(self.header.colnames)
   852→            if self.fill_include_names is not None:
   853→                colnames.intersection_update(self.fill_include_names)
   854→            if self.fill_exclude_names is not None:
   855→                colnames.difference_update(self.fill_exclude_names)
   856→
   857→            # Step 2a: Find out which columns are affected by this tuple
   858→            # iterate over reversed order, so last condition is set first and
   859→            # overwritten by earlier conditions
   860→            for replacement in reversed(self.fill_values):
   861→                if len(replacement) < 2:
   862→                    raise ValueError("Format of fill_values must be "

   941→def convert_numpy(numpy_type):
   942→    """Return a tuple containing a function which converts a list into a numpy
   943→    array and the type produced by the converter function.
   944→
   945→    Parameters
   946→    ----------
   947→    numpy_type : numpy data-type
   948→        The numpy type required of an array returned by ``converter``. Must be a
   949→        valid `numpy type <https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.types.html>`_
   950→        (e.g., numpy.uint, numpy.int8, numpy.int64, numpy.float64) or a python
   951→        type covered by a numpy type (e.g., int, float, str, bool).
   952→
   953→    Returns
   954→    -------
   955→    converter : callable
   956→        ``converter`` is a function which accepts a list and converts it to a
   957→        numpy array of type ``numpy_type``.
   958→    converter_type : type
   959→        ``converter_type`` tracks the generic data type produced by the
   960→        converter function.
   961→
   962→    Raises
   963→    ------
   964→    ValueError
   965→        Raised by ``converter`` if the list elements could not be converted to
   966→        the required type.
   967→    """
   968→
   969→    # Infer converter type from an instance of numpy_type.
   970→    type_name = numpy.array([], dtype=numpy_type).dtype.name
   971→    if 'int' in type_name:
   972→        converter_type = IntType
   973→    elif 'float' in type_name:
   974→        converter_type = FloatType
   975→    elif 'bool' in type_name:
   976→        converter_type = BoolType
   977→    elif 'str' in type_name:
   978→        converter_type = StrType
   979→    else:
   980→        converter_type = AllType
   981→
   982→    def bool_converter(vals):
   983→        """
   984→        Convert values "False" and "True" to bools.  Raise an exception
   985→        for any other string values.
   986→        """
   987→        if len(vals) == 0:
   988→            return numpy.array([], dtype=bool)
   989→
   990→        # Try a smaller subset first for a long array
   991→        if len(vals) > 10000:
   992→            svals = numpy.asarray(vals[:1000])
   993→            if not numpy.all((svals == 'False')
   994→                             | (svals == 'True')
   995→                             | (svals == '0')
   996→                             | (svals == '1')):
   997→                raise ValueError('bool input strings must be False, True, 0, 1, or ""')
   998→        vals = numpy.asarray(vals)
   999→
  1000→        trues = (vals == 'True') | (vals == '1')
  1001→        falses = (vals == 'False') | (vals == '0')
  1002→        if not numpy.all(trues | falses):
  1003→            raise ValueError('bool input strings must be only False, True, 0, 1, or ""')
  1004→
  1005→        return trues
  1006→
  1007→    def generic_converter(vals):
  1008→        return numpy.array(vals, numpy_type)
  1009→
  1010→    converter = bool_converter if converter_type is BoolType else generic_converter
  1011→
  1012→    return converter, converter_type

  1015→class BaseOutputter:
  1016→    """Output table as a dict of column objects keyed on column name.  The
  1017→    table data are stored as plain python lists within the column objects.
  1018→    """
  1019→    # User-defined converters which gets set in ascii.ui if a `converter` kwarg
  1020→    # is supplied.
  1021→    converters = {}
  1022→
  1023→    # Derived classes must define default_converters and __call__
  1024→
  1025→    @staticmethod
  1026→    def _validate_and_copy(col, converters):
  1027→        """Validate the format for the type converters and then copy those
  1028→        which are valid converters for this column (i.e. converter type is
  1029→        a subclass of col.type)"""
  1030→        # Allow specifying a single converter instead of a list of converters.
  1031→        # The input `converters` must be a ``type`` value that can init np.dtype.
  1032→        try:
  1033→            # Don't allow list-like things that dtype accepts
  1034→            assert type(converters) is type
  1035→            converters = [numpy.dtype(converters)]
  1036→        except (AssertionError, TypeError):
  1037→            pass
  1038→
  1039→        converters_out = []
  1040→        try:
  1041→            for converter in converters:
  1042→                try:
  1043→                    converter_func, converter_type = converter
  1044→                except TypeError as err:
  1045→                    if str(err).startswith('cannot unpack'):
  1046→                        converter_func, converter_type = convert_numpy(converter)
  1047→                    else:
  1048→                        raise
  1049→                if not issubclass(converter_type, NoType):
  1050→                    raise ValueError('converter_type must be a subclass of NoType')
  1051→                if issubclass(converter_type, col.type):
  1052→                    converters_out.append((converter_func, converter_type))
  1053→
  1054→        except (ValueError, TypeError) as err:
  1055→            raise ValueError('Error: invalid format for converters, see '
  1056→                             f'documentation\n{converters}: {err}')
  1057→        return converters_out
  1058→
  1059→    def _convert_vals(self, cols):
  1060→        for col in cols:
  1061→            for key, converters in self.converters.items():
  1062→                if fnmatch.fnmatch(col.name, key):
  1063→                    break
  1064→            else:
  1065→                if col.dtype is not None:
  1066→                    converters = [convert_numpy(col.dtype)]
  1067→                else:
  1068→                    converters = self.default_converters
  1069→
  1070→            col.converters = self._validate_and_copy(col, converters)
  1071→
  1072→            # Catch the last error in order to provide additional information
  1073→            # in case all attempts at column conversion fail.  The initial
  1074→            # value of of last_error will apply if no converters are defined
  1075→            # and the first col.converters[0] access raises IndexError.
  1076→            last_err = 'no converters defined'
  1077→
  1078→            while not hasattr(col, 'data'):
  1079→                # Try converters, popping the unsuccessful ones from the list.
  1080→                # If there are no converters left here then fail.
  1081→                if not col.converters:
  1082→                    raise ValueError(f'Column {col.name} failed to convert: {last_err}')
  1083→
  1084→                converter_func, converter_type = col.converters[0]
  1085→                if not issubclass(converter_type, col.type):
  1086→                    raise TypeError('converter type does not match column type')
  1087→
  1088→                try:
  1089→                    col.data = converter_func(col.str_vals)
  1090→                    col.type = converter_type
  1091→                except (TypeError, ValueError) as err:
  1092→                    col.converters.pop(0)
  1093→                    last_err = err
  1094→                except OverflowError as err:
  1095→                    # Overflow during conversion (most likely an int that
  1096→                    # doesn't fit in native C long). Put string at the top of
  1097→                    # the converters list for the next while iteration.
  1098→                    warnings.warn(
  1099→                        "OverflowError converting to {} in column {}, reverting to String."
  1100→                        .format(converter_type.__name__, col.name), AstropyWarning)
  1101→                    col.converters.insert(0, convert_numpy(numpy.str))
  1102→                    last_err = err

  1105→def _deduplicate_names(names):
  1106→    """Ensure there are no duplicates in ``names``
  1107→
  1108→    This is done by iteratively adding ``_<N>`` to the name for increasing N
  1109→    until the name is unique.
  1110→    """
  1111→    new_names = []
  1112→    existing_names = set()
  1113→
  1114→    for name in names:
  1115→        base_name = name + '_'
  1116→        i = 1
  1117→        while name in existing_names:
  1118→            # Iterate until a unique name is found
  1119→            name = base_name + str(i)
  1120→            i += 1
  1121→        new_names.append(name)
  1122→        existing_names.add(name)
  1123→
  1124→    return new_names

  1200→def _apply_include_exclude_names(table, names, include_names, exclude_names):
  1201→    """
  1202→    Apply names, include_names and exclude_names to a table or BaseHeader.
  1203→
  1204→    For the latter this relies on BaseHeader implementing ``colnames``,
  1205→    ``rename_column``, and ``remove_columns``.
  1206→
  1207→    Parameters
  1208→    ----------
  1209→    table : `~astropy.table.Table`, `~astropy.io.ascii.BaseHeader`
  1210→        Input table or BaseHeader subclass instance
  1211→    names : list
  1212→        List of names to override those in table (set to None to use existing names)
  1213→    include_names : list
  1214→        List of names to include in output
  1215→    exclude_names : list
  1216→        List of names to exclude from output (applied after ``include_names``)
  1217→
  1218→    """
  1219→    def rename_columns(table, names):
  1220→        # Rename table column names to those passed by user
  1221→        # Temporarily rename with names that are not in `names` or `table.colnames`.
  1222→        # This ensures that rename succeeds regardless of existing names.
  1223→        xxxs = 'x' * max(len(name) for name in list(names) + list(table.colnames))
  1224→        for ii, colname in enumerate(table.colnames):
  1225→            table.rename_column(colname, xxxs + str(ii))
  1226→
  1227→        for ii, name in enumerate(names):
  1228→            table.rename_column(xxxs + str(ii), name)
  1229→
  1230→    if names is not None:
  1231→        rename_columns(table, names)
  1232→    else:
  1233→        colnames_uniq = _deduplicate_names(table.colnames)
  1234→        if colnames_uniq != list(table.colnames):
  1235→            rename_columns(table, colnames_uniq)
  1236→
  1237→    names_set = set(table.colnames)
  1238→
  1239→    if include_names is not None:
  1240→        names_set.intersection_update(include_names)
  1241→    if exclude_names is not None:
  1242→        names_set.difference_update(exclude_names)
  1243→    if names_set != set(table.colnames):
  1244→        remove_names = set(table.colnames) - names_set
  1245→        table.remove_columns(remove_names)

  1248→class BaseReader(metaclass=MetaBaseReader):

   143→            arr_dtype = arr.dtype.byteorder + arr.dtype.kind + str(values_str_len)
   144→            arr = arr.astype(arr_dtype)

   149→def _convert_sequence_data_to_array(data, dtype=None):
   150→    """Convert N-d sequence-like data to ndarray or MaskedArray.
   151→
   152→    This is the core function for converting Python lists or list of lists to a
   153→    numpy array. This handles embedded np.ma.masked constants in ``data`` along
   154→    with the special case of an homogeneous list of MaskedArray elements.
   155→
   156→    Considerations:
   157→
   158→    - np.ma.array is about 50 times slower than np.array for list input. This
   159→      function avoids using np.ma.array on list input.
   160→    - np.array emits a UserWarning for embedded np.ma.masked, but only for int
   161→      or float inputs. For those it converts to np.nan and forces float dtype.
   162→      For other types np.array is inconsistent, for instance converting
   163→      np.ma.masked to "0.0" for str types.
   164→    - Searching in pure Python for np.ma.masked in ``data`` is comparable in
   165→      speed to calling ``np.array(data)``.
   166→    - This function may end up making two additional copies of input ``data``.
   167→
   168→    Parameters
   169→    ----------
   170→    data : N-d sequence
   171→        Input data, typically list or list of lists
   172→    dtype : None or dtype-like
   173→        Output datatype (None lets np.array choose)
   174→
   175→    Returns
   176→    -------
   177→    np_data : np.ndarray or np.ma.MaskedArray
   178→
   179→    """
   180→    np_ma_masked = np.ma.masked  # Avoid repeated lookups of this object
   181→
   182→    # Special case of an homogeneous list of MaskedArray elements (see #8977).
   183→    # np.ma.masked is an instance of MaskedArray, so exclude those values.
   184→    if (hasattr(data, '__len__')
   185→        and len(data) > 0
   186→        and all(isinstance(val, np.ma.MaskedArray)
   187→                and val is not np_ma_masked for val in data)):
   188→        np_data = np.ma.array(data, dtype=dtype)
   189→        return np_data
   190→
   191→    # First convert data to a plain ndarray. If there are instances of np.ma.masked
   192→    # in the data this will issue a warning for int and float.
   193→    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as warns:
   194→        # Ensure this warning from numpy is always enabled and that it is not
   195→        # converted to an error (which can happen during pytest).
   196→        warnings.filterwarnings('always', category=UserWarning,
   197→                                message='.*converting a masked element.*')
   198→        # FutureWarning in numpy 1.21. See https://github.com/astropy/astropy/issues/11291
   199→        # and https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/18425.
   200→        warnings.filterwarnings('always', category=FutureWarning,
   201→                                message='.*Promotion of numbers and bools to strings.*')
   202→        try:
   203→            np_data = np.array(data, dtype=dtype)
   204→        except np.ma.MaskError:
   205→            # Catches case of dtype=int with masked values, instead let it
   206→            # convert to float
   207→            np_data = np.array(data)
   208→        except Exception:
   209→            # Conversion failed for some reason, e.g. [2, 1*u.m] gives TypeError in Quantity.
   210→            # First try to interpret the data as Quantity. If that still fails then fall
   211→            # through to object
   212→            try:
   213→                np_data = Quantity(data, dtype)
   214→            except Exception:
   215→                dtype = object
   216→                np_data = np.array(data, dtype=dtype)
   217→
   218→    if np_data.ndim == 0 or (np_data.ndim > 0 and len(np_data) == 0):
   219→        # Implies input was a scalar or an empty list (e.g. initializing an
   220→        # empty table with pre-declared names and dtypes but no data).  Here we
   221→        # need to fall through to initializing with the original data=[].
   222→        return data
   223→
   224→    # If there were no warnings and the data are int or float, then we are done.
   225→    # Other dtypes like string or complex can have masked values and the
   226→    # np.array() conversion gives the wrong answer (e.g. converting np.ma.masked
   227→    # to the string "0.0").
   228→    if len(warns) == 0 and np_data.dtype.kind in ('i', 'f'):
   229→        return np_data
   230→
   231→    # Now we need to determine if there is an np.ma.masked anywhere in input data.
   232→
   233→    # Make a statement like below to look for np.ma.masked in a nested sequence.
   234→    # Because np.array(data) succeeded we know that `data` has a regular N-d
   235→    # structure. Find ma_masked:
   236→    #   any(any(any(d2 is ma_masked for d2 in d1) for d1 in d0) for d0 in data)
   237→    # Using this eval avoids creating a copy of `data` in the more-usual case of
   238→    # no masked elements.
   239→    any_statement = 'd0 is ma_masked'
   240→    for ii in reversed(range(np_data.ndim)):
   241→        if ii == 0:
   242→            any_statement = f'any({any_statement} for d0 in data)'
   243→        elif ii == np_data.ndim - 1:
   244→            any_statement = f'any(d{ii} is ma_masked for d{ii} in d{ii-1})'
   245→        else:
   246→            any_statement = f'any({any_statement} for d{ii} in d{ii-1})'
   247→    context = {'ma_masked': np.ma.masked, 'data': data}
   248→    has_masked = eval(any_statement, context)
   249→
   250→    # If there are any masks then explicitly change each one to a fill value and
   251→    # set a mask boolean array. If not has_masked then we're done.
   252→    if has_masked:
   253→        mask = np.zeros(np_data.shape, dtype=bool)
   254→        data_filled = np.array(data, dtype=object)
   255→
   256→        # Make type-appropriate fill value based on initial conversion.
   257→        if np_data.dtype.kind == 'U':
   258→            fill = ''
   259→        elif np_data.dtype.kind == 'S':
   260→            fill = b''
   261→        else:
   262→            # Zero works for every numeric type.
   263→            fill = 0
   264→
   265→        ranges = [range(dim) for dim in np_data.shape]
   266→        for idxs in itertools.product(*ranges):
   267→            val = data_filled[idxs]
   268→            if val is np_ma_masked:
   269→                data_filled[idxs] = fill
   270→                mask[idxs] = True
   271→            elif isinstance(val, bool) and dtype is None:
   272→                # If we see a bool and dtype not specified then assume bool for
   273→                # the entire array. Not perfect but in most practical cases OK.
   274→                # Unfortunately numpy types [False, 0] as int, not bool (and
   275→                # [False, np.ma.masked] => array([0.0, np.nan])).
   276→                dtype = bool
   277→
   278→        # If no dtype is provided then need to convert back to list so np.array
   279→        # does type autodetection.
   280→        if dtype is None:
   281→            data_filled = data_filled.tolist()
   282→
   283→        # Use np.array first to convert `data` to ndarray (fast) and then make
   284→        # masked array from an ndarray with mask (fast) instead of from `data`.
   285→        np_data = np.ma.array(np.array(data_filled, dtype=dtype), mask=mask)
   286→
   287→    return np_data

   290→def _make_compare(oper):
   291→    """
   292→    Make Column comparison methods which encode the ``other`` object to utf-8
   293→    in the case of a bytestring dtype for Py3+.
   294→
   295→    Parameters
   296→    ----------
   297→    oper : str
   298→        Operator name
   299→    """
   300→    def _compare(self, other):
   301→        op = oper  # copy enclosed ref to allow swap below
   302→
   303→        # If other is a Quantity, we should let it do the work, since
   304→        # it can deal with our possible unit (which, for MaskedColumn,
   305→        # would get dropped below, as '.data' is accessed in super()).
   306→        if isinstance(other, Quantity):
   307→            return NotImplemented
   308→
   309→        # If we are unicode and other is a column with bytes, defer to it for
   310→        # doing the unicode sandwich.  This avoids problems like those
   311→        # discussed in #6838 and #6899.
   312→        if (self.dtype.kind == 'U'
   313→                and isinstance(other, Column) and other.dtype.kind == 'S'):
   314→            return NotImplemented
   315→
   316→        # If we are bytes, encode other as needed.
   317→        if self.dtype.char == 'S':
   318→            other = self._encode_str(other)
   319→
   320→        # Now just let the regular ndarray.__eq__, etc., take over.
   321→        result = getattr(super(Column, self), op)(other)
   322→        # But we should not return Column instances for this case.
   323→        return result.data if isinstance(result, Column) else result
   324→
   325→    return _compare

   328→class ColumnInfo(BaseColumnInfo):
   329→    """
   330→    Container for meta information like name, description, format.
   331→
   332→    This is required when the object is used as a mixin column within a table,
   333→    but can be used as a general way to store meta information.
   334→    """
   335→    attr_names = BaseColumnInfo.attr_names | {'groups'}
   336→    _attrs_no_copy = BaseColumnInfo._attrs_no_copy | {'groups'}
   337→    attrs_from_parent = attr_names
   338→    _supports_indexing = True
   339→    # For structured columns, data is used to store a dict of columns.
   340→    # Store entries in that dict as name.key instead of name.data.key.
   341→    _represent_as_dict_primary_data = 'data'
   342→
   343→    def _represent_as_dict(self):
   344→        result = super()._represent_as_dict()
   345→        names = self._parent.dtype.names
   346→        # For a regular column, we are done, but for a structured
   347→        # column, we use a SerializedColumns to store the pieces.
   348→        if names is None:
   349→            return result
   350→
   351→        from .serialize import SerializedColumn
   352→
   353→        data = SerializedColumn()
   354→        # If this column has a StructuredUnit, we split it and store
   355→        # it on the corresponding part. Otherwise, we just store it
   356→        # as an attribute below.  All other attributes we remove from
   357→        # the parts, so that we do not store them multiple times.
   358→        # (Note that attributes are not linked to the parent, so it
   359→        # is safe to reset them.)
   360→        # TODO: deal with (some of) this in Column.__getitem__?
   361→        # Alternatively: should we store info on the first part?
   362→        # TODO: special-case format somehow? Can we have good formats
   363→        # for structured columns?
   364→        unit = self.unit
   365→        if isinstance(unit, StructuredUnit) and len(unit) == len(names):
   366→            units = unit.values()
   367→            unit = None  # No need to store as an attribute as well.
   368→        else:
   369→            units = [None] * len(names)
   370→        for name, part_unit in zip(names, units):
   371→            part = self._parent[name]
   372→            part.unit = part_unit
   373→            part.description = None
   374→            part.meta = {}
   375→            part.format = None
   376→            data[name] = part
   377→
   378→        # Create the attributes required to reconstruct the column.
   379→        result['data'] = data
   380→        # Store the shape if needed. Just like scalar data, a structured data
   381→        # column (e.g. with dtype `f8,i8`) can be multidimensional within each
   382→        # row and have a shape, and that needs to be distinguished from the
   383→        # case that each entry in the structure has the same shape (e.g.,
   384→        # distinguist a column with dtype='f8,i8' and 2 elements per row from
   385→        # one with dtype '2f8,2i8' and just one element per row).
   386→        if shape := self._parent.shape[1:]:
   387→            result['shape'] = list(shape)
   388→        # Also store the standard info attributes since these are
   389→        # stored on the parent and can thus just be passed on as
   390→        # arguments.  TODO: factor out with essentially the same
   391→        # code in serialize._represent_mixin_as_column.
   392→        if unit is not None and unit != '':
   393→            result['unit'] = unit
   394→        if self.format is not None:
   395→            result['format'] = self.format
   396→        if self.description is not None:
   397→            result['description'] = self.description
   398→        if self.meta:
   399→            result['meta'] = self.meta
   400→
   401→        return result

   403→    def _construct_from_dict(self, map):
   404→        if not isinstance(map.get('data'), dict):
   405→            return super()._construct_from_dict(map)
   406→
   407→        # Reconstruct a structured Column, by first making an empty column
   408→        # and then filling it with the structured data.
   409→        data = map.pop('data')
   410→        shape = tuple(map.pop('shape', ()))
   411→        # There are three elements in the shape of `part`:
   412→        # (table length, shape of structured column, shape of part like '3f8')
   413→        # The column `shape` only includes the second, so by adding one to its
   414→        # length to include the table length, we pick off a possible last bit.
   415→        dtype = np.dtype([(name, part.dtype, part.shape[len(shape)+1:])
   416→                          for name, part in data.items()])
   417→        units = tuple(col.info.unit for col in data.values())
   418→        if all(unit is not None for unit in units):
   419→            map['unit'] = StructuredUnit(units, dtype)
   420→        map.update(dtype=dtype, shape=shape, length=len(data[dtype.names[0]]))
   421→        # Construct the empty column from `map` (note: 'data' removed above).
   422→        result = super()._construct_from_dict(map)
   423→        # Fill it with the structured data.
   424→        for name in dtype.names:
   425→            result[name] = data[name]
   426→        return result

   561→    def copy(self, order='C', data=None, copy_data=True):
   562→        """
   563→        Return a copy of the current instance.
   564→
   565→        If ``data`` is supplied then a view (reference) of ``data`` is used,
   566→        and ``copy_data`` is ignored.
   567→

   569→        ----------

   571→            Controls the memory layout of the copy. 'C' means C-order,
   572→            'F' means F-order, 'A' means 'F' if ``a`` is Fortran contiguous,
   573→            'C' otherwise. 'K' means match the layout of ``a`` as closely
   574→            as possible. (Note that this function and :func:numpy.copy are very
   575→            similar, but have different default values for their order=
   576→            arguments.)  Default is 'C'.

   579→            data.  This allows copying the instance attributes and meta.
   580→        copy_data : bool, optional

   582→            reference.  Default is True.

   585→        -------

   587→            Copy of the current column (same type as original)

   598→        # implies complete independence from original).  __array_finalize__ will have already
   599→        # made a light copy.  I'm not sure how to avoid that initial light copy.
   600→        if self.meta is not None:

   604→        # from self, which is not the idea here, so undo
   605→        if isinstance(self, MaskedColumn):

   612→    def __setstate__(self, state):
   613→        """
   614→        Restore the internal state of the Column/MaskedColumn for pickling
   615→        purposes.  This requires that the last element of ``state`` is a
   616→        5-tuple that has Column-specific state values.
   617→        """
   618→        # Get the Column attributes
   619→        names = ('_name', '_unit', '_format', 'description', 'meta', 'indices')
   620→        attrs = {name: val for name, val in zip(names, state[-1])}
   621→
   622→        state = state[:-1]
   623→
   624→        # Using super().__setstate__(state) gives
   625→        # "TypeError 'int' object is not iterable", raised in
   626→        # astropy.table._column_mixins._ColumnGetitemShim.__setstate_cython__()
   627→        # Previously, it seems to have given an infinite recursion.
   628→        # Hence, manually call the right super class to actually set up
   629→        # the array object.
   630→        super_class = ma.MaskedArray if isinstance(self, ma.MaskedArray) else np.ndarray
   631→        super_class.__setstate__(self, state)
   632→
   633→        # Set the Column attributes
   634→        for name, val in attrs.items():
   635→            setattr(self, name, val)

   638→    def __reduce__(self):
   639→        """
   640→        Return a 3-tuple for pickling a Column.  Use the super-class
   641→        functionality but then add in a 5-tuple of Column-specific values
   642→        that get used in __setstate__.
   643→        """
   644→        super_class = ma.MaskedArray if isinstance(self, ma.MaskedArray) else np.ndarray
   645→        reconstruct_func, reconstruct_func_args, state = super_class.__reduce__(self)
   646→
   647→        # Define Column-specific attrs and meta that gets added to state.
   648→        column_state = (self.name, self.unit, self.format, self.description,
   649→                        self.meta, self.indices)
   650→        state = state + (column_state,)
   651→
   652→        return reconstruct_func, reconstruct_func_args, state

   654→    def __array_finalize__(self, obj):
   655→        # Obj will be none for direct call to Column() creator
   656→        if obj is None:
   657→            return
   658→
   659→        if callable(super().__array_finalize__):
   660→            super().__array_finalize__(obj)
   661→
   662→        # Self was created from template (e.g. obj[slice] or (obj * 2))
   663→        # or viewcast e.g. obj.view(Column).  In either case we want to
   664→        # init Column attributes for self from obj if possible.
   665→        self.parent_table = None
   666→        if not hasattr(self, 'indices'):  # may have been copied in __new__
   667→            self.indices = []
   668→        self._copy_attrs(obj)
   669→        if 'info' in getattr(obj, '__dict__', {}):
   670→            self.info = obj.info

   672→    def __array_wrap__(self, out_arr, context=None):
   673→        """
   674→        __array_wrap__ is called at the end of every ufunc.
   675→
   676→        Normally, we want a Column object back and do not have to do anything
   677→        special. But there are two exceptions:
   678→
   679→        1) If the output shape is different (e.g. for reduction ufuncs
   680→           like sum() or mean()), a Column still linking to a parent_table
   681→           makes little sense, so we return the output viewed as the
   682→           column content (ndarray or MaskedArray).

  1060→    @staticmethod
  1061→    def _encode_str(value):
  1062→        """
  1063→        Encode anything that is unicode-ish as utf-8.  This method is only
  1064→        called for Py3+.
  1065→        """
  1066→        if isinstance(value, str):
